title: Cross-Anesthetic ECoG State Decoding Fails at the Decision Threshold, Not the Representation
summary: Decoders of anesthetic state from cortical activity fail across drug classes, most notoriously ketamine, but reported accuracy cannot say whether the neural representation or only the decision threshold has failed; we separate the two in a controlled preparation with ground-truth labels. We decoded awake versus anesthetized from mouse electrocorticography (the 250-Hz-bandlimited local field potential, sampled at 1875 Hz) under leave-one-anesthetic-out evaluation across five mechanistically distinct anesthetics (isoflurane, dexmedetomidine, ketamine, propofol, and midazolam), comparing a spatially blind band-power decoder, covariance/Riemannian representations, and Riemannian domain adaptation, with all statistics at the session level and mouse-level cluster bootstrapping for the ketamine fold. The representation transfers: band-power ranks awake versus anesthetized at a session AUROC of at least 0.96 on every held-out drug, ketamine included (0.980, cluster confidence interval 0.821 to 1.000). The failure is confined to the threshold: across three representations the ketamine ranking is near-invariant while its balanced accuracy swings from chance to high, and a permutation test is significant for ranking (p = 0.0025) but not for fixed-threshold accuracy (p = 0.3795). Riemannian domain adaptation is net-negative. A causal, label-free threshold anchored to the subject's own pre-induction baseline fixes ketamine (balanced accuracy 0.50 to 0.85) and dominates domain adaptation. Because the ketamine test sessions come from three mice that also contribute training drugs, this is within-subject cross-drug transfer; we do not claim population-level transfer across subjects. In cross-drug state decoding the actionable failure is calibration, not representation.

AI.tldr: Cross-drug anesthetic state decoding from mouse ECoG fails not because neural representations don't transfer, but because decision thresholds do. Band-power features rank awake vs. anesthetized reliably across five anesthetics (including ketamine, AUROC 0.980), while fixed-threshold accuracy collapses. A label-free threshold anchored to the subject's own pre-induction baseline fixes ketamine calibration and outperforms Riemannian domain adaptation.
AI.motivation: Decoders of anesthetic state trained on cortical activity often fail when tested on unseen drugs, most notably ketamine, but prior work cannot distinguish whether the underlying neural representation fails to generalize or only the classification threshold is miscalibrated. Disentangling these two failure modes is essential for building robust, generalizable anesthetic-state monitors.
AI.method: Using a controlled mouse preparation with ground-truth labels, the authors decode awake vs. anesthetized from 1875 Hz-sampled ECoG (250 Hz bandlimited) under leave-one-anesthetic-out evaluation across five mechanistically distinct anesthetics: isoflurane, dexmedetomidine, ketamine, propofol, and midazolam. They compare a spatially blind band-power decoder, covariance/Riemannian representations, and Riemannian domain adaptation, reporting statistics at the session level with mouse-level cluster bootstrapping for the ketamine fold. They also test a causal, label-free threshold anchored to the subject's own pre-induction baseline.
AI.result: The representation transfers: band-power achieves session AUROC ≥0.96 on every held-out drug, including ketamine (0.980, cluster CI 0.821–1.000). The failure is confined to the threshold: ketamine ranking is near-invariant across representations while balanced accuracy swings from chance to high; a permutation test is significant for ranking (p=0.0025) but not fixed-threshold accuracy (p=0.3795). Riemannian domain adaptation is net-negative, while the baseline-anchored threshold improves ketamine balanced accuracy from 0.50 to 0.85 and dominates domain adaptation.
AI.conclusion: The paper concludes that in cross-drug anesthetic state decoding, the actionable failure is calibration, not representation. Ketamine test sessions come from mice that also contributed training drugs, so this is within-subject cross-drug transfer; population-level transfer across subjects is not claimed.

title: A Blind Spot in Alignment: Quantifying Biosecurity Risks in Large Language Models
summary: Large Language Models (LLMs) are accelerating biological research, yet this same capability poses a critical biosecurity threat: models that assist in protein engineering can equally be prompted to generate predicted toxin-like sequences, potentially lowering the barrier to biological misuse. Current safety evaluations, however, operate in natural language and cannot determine whether a model-generated amino acid sequence is biological gibberish or a computational risk signal. To address this evaluation blind spot, we introduce SPIKE-Bench, coupling 631 curated toxin-design prompts across seven functional categories with the SPIKE funnel, a three-stage protocol that filters output through compliance, biological plausibility, and predicted toxicity, producing stage-level diagnostics and an aggregate function-aware metric: the Functional Harmfulness Rate (FHR). An audit of 32 LLMs reveals that most models freely comply with toxin-design requests; FHR is driven primarily by biological generation capability rather than safety alignment, reaching 50.7%; and Refusal Rate fails to predict functional risk. As a first step toward mitigation, we provide BioSafe-Guard, a domain-specialized classifier that substantially reduces predicted functional risk while preserving benign utility. We release SPIKE-Bench and BioSafe-Guard at https://github.com/PKU-Alignment/SPIKE-Bench to support more rigorous biosecurity evaluation of LLMs.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces SPIKE-Bench, a benchmark for evaluating LLM biosecurity risks in protein engineering, coupled with a three-stage filtering protocol (SPIKE funnel) and a new metric (Functional Harmfulness Rate). An audit of 32 LLMs shows most freely comply with toxin-design requests, achieving up to 50.7% FHR, and that safety alignment fails to predict functional risk. The authors also provide BioSafe-Guard, a domain-specialized classifier that reduces functional risk while preserving utility.
AI.motivation: Current safety evaluations of LLMs operate in natural language and cannot determine whether a model-generated amino acid sequence is biologically meaningful or poses a genuine computational biosecurity risk, leaving a critical blind spot in assessing the threat of LLMs being used to generate toxin-like sequences.
AI.method: SPIKE-Bench includes 631 curated toxin-design prompts across seven functional categories. The SPIKE funnel is a three-stage protocol that filters generated outputs through compliance, biological plausibility, and predicted toxicity, producing stage-level diagnostics and the aggregate Functional Harmfulness Rate (FHR) metric.
AI.result: An audit of 32 LLMs found most models freely comply with toxin-design requests; FHR is driven primarily by biological generation capability rather than safety alignment, reaching 50.7%; and the Refusal Rate fails to predict functional risk. BioSafe-Guard substantially reduces predicted functional risk while preserving benign utility.
AI.conclusion: SPIKE-Bench and BioSafe-Guard are released publicly to support more rigorous biosecurity evaluation of LLMs, representing a first step toward mitigation of LLM-enabled biological misuse.

title: A method for comparing inferred evolutionary accumulation dynamics across covariates and model structures
summary: In this note we describe a method for comparing inferred dynamics in evolutionary accumulation models (EvAMs). These models involve the acquisition of multiple, potentially codependent, binary features over time -- for example, mutations in cancer development, or phenotypes in evolutionary biology. As the set of methods for inferring EvAM dynamics expands, approaches for comparing inference across algorithms, datasets, and covariates are required. In particular, a comparison method supporting reversible, stochastic dynamics, interactions between feature sets, and potentially non-independent samples (as well as simpler cases) has yet to be established. It is possible for EvAM with similar relative feature orderings to produce completely different sets of observed states due to ``frameshift''-like differences; methods distinguishing state and transition similarity are therefore also desirable. Here we suggest a method focussed on ordering matrices, describing the probability that a feature is acquired under different conditions on other features, and is thus generally comparable across methods and datasets. We demonstrate how the approach captures both statistical robustness (given EvAM uncertainty) and scientifically meaningful differences in inferred dynamics. The method is applied to synthetic and real-world data on the evolution of chromosomal aberrations in different tumour types and of drug-resistant bacteria in different countries.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a method for comparing inferred dynamics in evolutionary accumulation models (EvAMs), based on ordering matrices that describe feature acquisition probabilities under different conditions. This approach is generally comparable across methods and datasets, capturing both statistical robustness and scientifically meaningful differences, with applications to chromosomal aberrations in tumors and drug-resistant bacteria.
AI.motivation: As methods for inferring EvAM dynamics expand, there is a need for approaches to compare inference across algorithms, datasets, and covariates. No existing comparison method supports reversible, stochastic dynamics, interactions between feature sets, and non-independent samples simultaneously, and methods distinguishing state versus transition similarity are lacking.
AI.method: The approach is focused on ordering matrices that describe the probability a feature is acquired under different conditions on other features, making it generally comparable across methods and datasets.
AI.result: The method captures both statistical robustness (given EvAM uncertainty) and scientifically meaningful differences in inferred dynamics. It is applied to synthetic and real-world data on chromosomal aberration evolution in different tumor types and drug-resistant bacteria across different countries.
AI.conclusion: The proposed ordering-matrix-based comparison method addresses the need for comparing EvAM dynamics, supporting complex scenarios (reversible stochastic dynamics, feature interactions, non-independent samples) while distinguishing state and transition similarity.

title: REDE: A Quantitative Framework for Differential-Expression Reproducibility and Diagnostic Transfer Across Nine Cohorts and Three Cancers
comment: 44 pages, 7 main figures, 9 supplementary tables, and 8 supplementary figures. Code: https://github.com/Bluesman79/REDE-transcriptomic-reproducibility. Archived software release: https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.21774116
summary:
Differential-expression analyses often turn cohort-specific significance into claims of stable gene signatures or diagnostic biomarkers. We evaluated which layers of evidence reproduce across independent datasets and whether discovery-derived panels retain locked tumor-versus-non-tumor classification performance.
  Nine public microarray cohorts were organized into fixed discovery, validation, and external-test experiments for pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma, breast cancer, and lung cancer. Reproducibility was assessed for DEG burden, exact membership, top-rank overlap, signed effects, prespecified gene confirmation, and Hallmark pathways. We also introduced REDE-2Fold, in which each discovery cohort is split once at patient level, differential expression is performed independently in both folds, and only same-direction genes selected in both are retained. Four training-only panels were then evaluated with locked logistic models and thresholds: all discovery DEGs, the top 19 discovery DEGs, all REDE-2Fold genes, and the top 19 REDE-2Fold genes.
  Broad DEG-list confirmation in both independent cohorts ranged from 15.5% to 39.5%, rising to 50.1% to 84.3% for large effects. Pathway replication ranged from 52.2% to 88.9%. Compact 19-gene panels retained high external ROC-AUC, but locked operating points were often unstable: some models with ROC-AUC near 1.0 showed zero specificity or very low sensitivity.
  These results define a hierarchy from thresholded membership through effect, pathway, discrimination, and operating-point transfer. REDE provides a seven-level quantitative framework for matching transcriptomic claims to the evidence actually tested, while REDE-2Fold offers a minimum internal feature-stability procedure that strengthens but does not replace independent validation.

AI.tldr: This study systematically evaluates the reproducibility of differential-expression findings across independent cancer cohorts, introduces REDE-2Fold (a patient-level split-stability procedure), and shows that while compact gene panels retain high external discrimination (ROC-AUC), their locked operating points (thresholds) are often unstable—revealing a hierarchy of evidence from DEG membership through effect size, pathways, discrimination, to operating-point transfer.
AI.motivation: Differential-expression analyses often overstate the stability and clinical utility of gene signatures derived from cohort-specific data. The authors aim to quantify which layers of evidence actually reproduce across independent datasets and whether discovery-derived panels preserve locked classification performance.
AI.method: Nine public microarray cohorts for pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma, breast cancer, and lung cancer were organized into fixed discovery, validation, and external-test splits. Reproducibility was assessed across multiple dimensions (DEG burden, membership, top-rank overlap, signed effects, gene confirmation, Hallmark pathways). A new procedure called REDE-2Fold splits each discovery cohort once at patient level, runs differential expression independently in both folds, and retains only same-direction genes selected in both. Four training-only panels (all DEGs, top-19 DEGs, all REDE-2Fold genes, top-19 REDE-2Fold genes) were evaluated with locked logistic models and thresholds.
AI.result: Broad DEG-list confirmation across independent cohorts ranged 15.5%–39.5% (rising to 50.1%–84.3% for large-effect genes). Pathway replication ranged 52.2%–88.9%. Compact 19-gene panels maintained high external ROC-AUC, but locked operating points were often unstable—some models with ROC-AUC near 1.0 showed zero specificity or very low sensitivity.
AI.conclusion: The findings define an evidence hierarchy from thresholded membership through effect, pathway, discrimination, and operating-point transfer. REDE provides a seven-level quantitative framework for matching transcriptomic claims to tested evidence, and REDE-2Fold offers a minimum internal feature-stability procedure that strengthens but does not replace independent validation.

title: Detecting high-frequency brain disorder signals using dynamic mode decomposition from EEG
summary: Recent studies have reported clearly identifiable dynamical changes in the high-frequency range of EEG signals recorded during specific stimuli, such as visual or auditory inputs, or in cases of brain disorders like epileptic seizures. In this study, we utilized Dynamic Mode Decomposition (DMD) to extract consistent and persistent dynamical changes in the high-frequency band from the signals of neurologically relevant EEG channels. High-frequency DMD modes were employed as features, composing a feature table. Through post-processing, a random distribution test was performed, revealing that approximately 70% of the samples exhibited consistent high-frequency dynamics within the signal of a specific channel. Furthermore, classification experiments confirmed that the PCA components of the feature table that passed the test formed a consistent pattern that distinguished the alcohol-dependent group from the control group.

AI.tldr: This study applies Dynamic Mode Decomposition (DMD) to extract consistent high-frequency dynamical patterns from EEG signals, showing that ~70% of samples exhibit consistent high-frequency dynamics in specific channels, and PCA components of validated features can distinguish alcohol-dependent subjects from controls.
AI.motivation: Recent findings show identifiable dynamical changes in high-frequency EEG ranges during stimuli and neurological disorders, yet extracting consistent and persistent high-frequency dynamics from EEG signals remains challenging and underexplored.
AI.method: High-frequency DMD modes are extracted from neurologically relevant EEG channels as features to form a feature table. Post-processing includes a random distribution test to assess consistency, followed by PCA-based classification experiments on the surviving features.
AI.result: The random distribution test showed that approximately 70% of samples exhibited consistent high-frequency dynamics in a specific channel. Classification experiments confirmed that PCA components of validated features formed a consistent pattern distinguishing alcohol-dependent subjects from the control group.
AI.conclusion: DMD-based high-frequency features provide a reliable and consistent approach for identifying dynamical EEG patterns, with demonstrated discriminative power for alcohol dependence classification.

title: Expanding Protein Structure Prediction into Conformational State Space
summary: Recent AI advances have enabled protein structure prediction at near-experimental accuracy, largely solving the problem of identifying a dominant conformation from sequence. Many proteins, however, function as dynamic systems populating multiple conformational states with activity emerging from shifts in relative occupancy--an incomplete picture when reduced to one structure. Here, we argue that structure prediction should be reformulated as a state-space inference problem: recovering not one conformation's coordinates but accessible states, their energetic and kinetic relationships, context dependence, and responses to perturbations. We review emerging strategies--deep learning ensemble generators, physics-based simulations, and experimental constraints--and outline a roadmap toward state-space prediction.

AI.tldr: This paper argues that protein structure prediction should be reformulated from predicting a single dominant conformation to predicting the full state-space of a protein—including its accessible conformational states, their energetic and kinetic relationships, context dependence, and responses to perturbations—since many proteins function as dynamic systems where activity emerges from shifts in state occupancy.
AI.motivation: While AI has achieved near-experimental accuracy in predicting a single dominant protein structure, this is insufficient because many proteins are dynamic systems that populate multiple conformational states, and their biological function emerges from shifts in the relative occupancy of these states rather than a single static structure.
AI.method: The paper proposes reformulating structure prediction as a state-space inference problem and reviews emerging strategies including deep learning ensemble generators, physics-based simulations, and experimental constraints, along with a roadmap toward achieving state-space prediction.
AI.result: The paper presents a conceptual framework and roadmap for shifting protein structure prediction from single-structure to state-space prediction, discussing the integration of deep learning, physics-based simulations, and experimental data.
AI.conclusion: Protein structure prediction should evolve to recover not just one conformation's coordinates but the full accessible state-space of proteins—states, energetic/kinetic relationships, context dependence, and perturbation responses—to properly capture the dynamic nature underlying protein function.

title: Persistent homology broadens the controllable subspace in human structural connectomes
summary: Network control theory applied to structural connectomes typically ranks brain regions as candidate driver nodes by their structural connectivity strength, and evaluates performance through scalar control energy. We test whether this framing captures the most relevant information about how driver-node selection shapes brain network control. We introduce an alternative criterion based on the persistent topological cycles in which each node participates---a measure of mesoscale integration that captures features beyond local connectivity---and compare it to standard degree-based selection across 70 human structural connectomes at three parcellation scales. Topology- and degree-informed driver sets achieve nearly identical scalar control energy, differing by approximately 0.2%. The geometry of the controllable subspace, however, differs substantially: topology-informed sets distribute controllability across more dimensions of state space and produce better-conditioned controllability matrices. This geometric advantage is preserved when high-degree hub nodes are removed, and it carries a functional signature: because the two criteria place driver nodes in different cortical territory, each most efficiently reaches a different class of target state. The choice of node-ranking criterion therefore shapes which brain-state transitions are energetically favored even when average control cost is unchanged. The results reveal a dissociation between control cost and control geometry, and demonstrate that persistent topology captures information about brain network control that scalar energy summaries miss.

AI.tldr: This paper shows that while topology- and degree-based driver node selection in human structural connectomes achieve nearly identical scalar control energy (≈0.2% difference), they differ substantially in control geometry—topology-informed sets distribute controllability across more dimensions and yield better-conditioned controllability matrices. This geometric advantage persists even when hub nodes are removed and carries functional significance, as the two criteria place drivers in different cortical territory, each favoring different brain-state transitions.
AI.motivation: Standard network control theory ranks driver nodes in brain connectomes by structural connectivity strength (degree) and evaluates performance through scalar control energy. The authors question whether this framing captures the most relevant information about how driver-node selection shapes brain network control, and propose testing whether alternative criteria reveal information that scalar energy summaries miss.
AI.method: The authors introduce a topology-based criterion using persistent topological cycles in which each node participates—a measure of mesoscale integration capturing features beyond local connectivity. They compare this to standard degree-based selection across 70 human structural connectomes at three parcellation scales, and additionally test the case where high-degree hub nodes are removed.
AI.result: Topology- and degree-informed driver sets achieve nearly identical scalar control energy (~0.2% difference), but the controllable subspace geometry differs substantially: topology-informed sets distribute controllability across more state-space dimensions and produce better-conditioned controllability matrices. This geometric advantage persists without hub nodes and carries functional consequences—each criterion places drivers in different cortical territory, favoring different classes of target states.
AI.conclusion: The choice of node-ranking criterion shapes which brain-state transitions are energetically favored even when average control cost is unchanged. The results reveal a dissociation between control cost and control geometry, demonstrating that persistent topology captures information about brain network control that scalar energy summaries miss.

title: Stochastic partial differential equation model for environmental DNA dynamics in river environments
summary: Environmental DNA (eDNA) has emerged as a novel tool for quantifying the seasonal abundance of aquatic species in water bodies; however, its mathematical modeling is still at a germinating stage because of its mechanistic uncertainties. We propose a first-step mathematical and computational framework for the eDNA dynamics of migratory fish based on a novel stochastic partial differential equation model with a delayed source input. The model governs spatiotemporal eDNA concentration in rivers where the source comes from a stochastic differential equation for the migration dynamics of the fish. The affine nature of the model facilitates its theoretical analysis, including the guarantee of well-posedness and the closed-form derivation of the Laplace functional despite the proportionality coefficient of the multiplicative noise term being non-Lipschitz. We also propose a discretization scheme for the model that theoretically generates nonnegative numerical solutions. We finally apply the proposed model to eDNA concentration data sampled from midstream reaches of a river system and perform sensitivity analysis.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes a novel stochastic partial differential equation (SPDE) model with delayed source input to mathematically describe environmental DNA (eDNA) dynamics of migratory fish in rivers, including theoretical analysis, numerical discretization, and application to real eDNA concentration data with sensitivity analysis.
AI.motivation: eDNA is an emerging tool for quantifying seasonal abundance of aquatic species, but its mathematical modeling is still in its infancy due to mechanistic uncertainties about how eDNA moves and degrades in water bodies.
AI.method: The authors develop a first-step mathematical and computational framework using an SPDE model with a delayed source input. The source term is governed by a stochastic differential equation modeling fish migration dynamics. The affine structure of the model enables closed-form derivation of the Laplace functional and well-posedness guarantees, even though the multiplicative noise coefficient is non-Lipschitz. A discretization scheme is proposed that theoretically produces nonnegative numerical solutions.
AI.result: The model is applied to real eDNA concentration data from midstream reaches of a river system, and a sensitivity analysis is performed to understand how model parameters affect the eDNA dynamics.
AI.conclusion: The proposed framework represents a foundational step toward quantitative modeling of eDNA dynamics in aquatic environments, bridging stochastic modeling theory with practical eDNA monitoring applications.

title: Synergy and Complementarity: The Generative Basis of Chemical Organizations
summary:
Identifying structural features ensuring the persistence of a reaction network is fundamental for understanding the evolution and complexification of biological entities. By defining organizations as subsets of species that are closed and self-maintaining, Chemical Organization Theory (COT) shows that organizations enable filtering out the regions of the phase space where attractors can exist. Despite various theoretical explorations current methods to compute the organizations face unclear combinatorial challenges.
  In this article, we first perform a systematic study of such combinatorial challenges and identify a criteria of productive novelty and irreducibility that separate relevant from redundant combinations. Second, we identify the minimal building blocks that shall be combined to build organizations, called elementary reaction closures (ERC), and characterize them as a hierarchy. Third, we show that all persistent modules can be generated as combination of ERCs only, and operationalize two properties among ERCs, synergy and complementarity, that define a sufficient criteria to build such generators in a minimal way. Fourth we show that every relevant persistent module can be built from such minimal sequences of ERCs.
  We next show that the synergies and complementarities we use to generate persistent modules not only scale radically slower than usual combinatorial methods. We quantify these structures across $438$ biological reaction networks from the BioModels and BiGG databases. The proportion of fundamental synergies and complementarities among all ERC pairs shrinks as networks grow even as raw counts increase, confirming that larger biological networks achieve persistence through a progressively smaller and more selective sets.
  We do not prescribe algorithms to compute organizations, discuss how algorithms based on our results could permit applying COT.

AI.tldr: This paper addresses the combinatorial challenges in computing organizations within Chemical Organization Theory (COT) by introducing elementary reaction closures (ERCs) as minimal building blocks. The authors characterize ERCs hierarchically, show all persistent modules can be generated from them, and define synergy and complementarity properties that enable minimal generation. They validate their approach on 438 biological reaction networks, demonstrating that the proportion of fundamental synergies/complementarities shrinks as networks grow, suggesting larger networks achieve persistence through increasingly selective sets.
AI.motivation: To overcome the unclear combinatorial challenges in computing organizations in Chemical Organization Theory (COT), which are essential for filtering regions of phase space where attractors can exist, thereby understanding the evolution and complexification of biological entities.
AI.method: The authors systematically study the combinatorial challenges in computing organizations, identifying criteria of productive novelty and irreducibility. They define elementary reaction closures (ERCs) as minimal building blocks characterized hierarchically. They operationalize synergy and complementarity properties among ERCs to define sufficient criteria for generating persistent modules minimally, and validate their approach on 438 biological reaction networks from BioModels and BiGG databases.
AI.result: The synergy and complementarity approach scales radically slower than usual combinatorial methods. Quantitative analysis across 438 biological networks shows that the proportion of fundamental synergies and complementarities shrinks as networks grow, even though raw counts increase, confirming that larger biological networks achieve persistence through progressively smaller and more selective sets.
AI.conclusion: The paper establishes ERCs as minimal building blocks for generating persistent modules and demonstrates that the proposed synergy/complementarity framework offers a scalable approach to COT. The findings suggest potential algorithmic improvements for computing organizations, though no specific algorithms are prescribed.

title: Identifiability of phylogenetic networks and quintet concordance factors
summary: Several statistical methods of phylogenetic network inference and testing for non-tree-like relationships are based on assessing genomic data through quartet Concordance Factors, the frequencies of 4-taxon topological relationships on gene trees. While such an approach obviates making several undesirable modeling assumptions, it also results in non-identifiability issues for network roots and for small cycles. In this work, an algorithm and accompanying Macaulay2 implementation are provided for computing $n$-tet Concordance Factors on any phylogenetic network. We employ this algorithm on quintet Concordance Factors, summarizing 5-taxon gene trees, to explore identifiability of level-1 networks under the Network Multispecies Coalescent model. We show some additional network features become identifiable that are not through quartets. As identifiability is a necessary prerequisite to inference by any method, this lays a foundation for future inference work.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces an algorithm and Macaulay2 implementation for computing n-taxon Concordance Factors on phylogenetic networks, applied to quintet Concordance Factors (5-taxon gene tree frequencies) under the Network Multispecies Coalescent model to explore identifiability of level-1 networks.
AI.motivation: Quartet Concordance Factors are commonly used in phylogenetic network inference but suffer from non-identifiability issues, particularly for network roots and small cycles. The authors aim to extend beyond quartets to improve the identifiability of network features.
AI.method: The authors develop an algorithm with a Macaulay2 implementation to compute n-taxon Concordance Factors on any phylogenetic network, and apply it to quintet Concordance Factors (summarizing 5-taxon gene trees) to analyze identifiability of level-1 networks under the Network Multispecies Coalescent model.
AI.result: Using quintet Concordance Factors, the authors show that some additional network features become identifiable that are not identifiable through quartets, addressing some of the non-identifiability issues present in quartet-based approaches.
AI.conclusion: Since identifiability is a necessary prerequisite for inference by any method, establishing these new identifiability results with quintets lays a foundation for future phylogenetic network inference work.

title: Population Structures with Positive Feedback and Asymmetric Division
summary: In bioreactor experiments, budding yeast can manifest stable metabolic oscillations. In some instances these oscillations involve the cell cycle and are associated with a dynamical phenomenon called temporal clustering. Since yeast divide asymmetrically, mother cells may be able to divide sooner than the smaller daughter cells. We show that asymmetric division plus positive feedback can result in stable temporal clustering. In this scenario, the cells self-organize into $p$ clusters of mother cells and $q$ clusters of daughter cells, $p \le q$. In simple numerical simulations of a population model with asymmetric division and positive feedback, we show that $p:q$ periodic arrangements form spontaneously from random populations of cells. Our main result is that these structures can be stable.

AI.tldr: This paper demonstrates that asymmetric cell division combined with positive feedback can produce stable temporal clustering in budding yeast populations, leading to self-organized p:q periodic arrangements of mother and daughter cell clusters.
AI.motivation: Budding yeast exhibit stable metabolic oscillations in bioreactors, some involving the cell cycle with a phenomenon called temporal clustering. Understanding what drives this clustering is important, and since yeast divide asymmetrically (mothers can divide sooner than daughters), the authors investigate whether this asymmetry, combined with positive feedback, can explain stable clustering patterns.
AI.method: The authors develop a population model incorporating asymmetric division and positive feedback, then run numerical simulations showing that p:q periodic arrangements (p clusters of mother cells, q clusters of daughter cells, with p ≤ q) form spontaneously from initially random cell populations.
AI.result: Simulations show that p:q periodic arrangements spontaneously emerge from random populations under asymmetric division with positive feedback. The main result is that these self-organized structures can be stable.
AI.conclusion: Asymmetric division plus positive feedback is sufficient to produce stable temporal clustering in budding yeast populations, providing a mechanistic explanation for the p:q clustering structures observed in bioreactor experiments.

title: The Zombie Infection Model
comment: 56 pages, 12 figures. Submitted to the Electronic Journal of Probability
summary: We study a variant of the stochastic SIR model on graphs that has previously been introduced in the physics literature for modelling zombie outbreaks and here referred to as the Zombie Infection Model (ZIM). In this model, initially each node of a graph is either susceptible, infected or removed. As in the SIR model, a susceptible node becomes infected at rate $λ$ times the number of its infected neighbours. Moreover, in the ZIM, an infected node is removed at rate $1$ times the number of its susceptible neighbours. This process exhibits rich and sometimes counterintuitive behaviour. By combining various coupling techniques, we provide a rigorous mathematical analysis of the model, focusing on monotonicity properties and the probability of the infection spreading indefinitely. One of our main results is that this probability is monotone with respect to an increase of $λ$ for the process on trees, but that there are graphs of bounded degree for which it is continuous and yet not monotone. We also establish bounds on this probability for the process on general graphs, and derive more precise results for complete graphs, regular trees, and the $d$-dimensional integer lattice.

AI.tldr: This paper provides a rigorous mathematical analysis of the Zombie Infection Model (ZIM), a variant of the stochastic SIR model on graphs where infected nodes are removed at a rate proportional to the number of susceptible neighbors. The authors study monotonicity properties and extinction probability of infection, proving that on trees the probability of indefinite spread is monotone in λ, while on bounded-degree graphs it can be continuous yet non-monotone. They also derive bounds and precise results for complete graphs, regular trees, and the d-dimensional lattice.
AI.motivation: The ZIM, despite being introduced in physics literature for zombie outbreaks, exhibits rich and counterintuitive behaviors that lack rigorous mathematical analysis. The authors aim to provide a solid theoretical foundation for understanding the infection spread dynamics in this model.
AI.method: The paper employs various coupling techniques to analyze the model, focusing on monotonicity properties and the probability of infection spreading indefinitely across different graph topologies.
AI.result: The main results show that (1) the probability of indefinite spread is monotone in λ on trees, (2) there exist bounded-degree graphs where this probability is continuous but not monotone, and (3) bounds on this probability are established for general graphs with more precise results obtained for complete graphs, regular trees, and the d-dimensional integer lattice.
AI.conclusion: The analysis reveals that the ZIM exhibits non-trivial, sometimes counterintuitive behavior depending on the underlying graph structure, with monotonicity properties that are sensitive to graph topology.

title: Predictive Set Theory: A Generative Framework for Cognitive Architecture with Operationalized Core Mechanisms
comment: 103 pages. This preprint establishes the theoretical framework of Predictive Set Theory, providing a generative design specification for cognitive architecture. Comments welcome
summary: Predictive processing theories portray the brain as a hierarchical prediction engine that minimizes prediction error, yet they lack operational definitions for the structure of a "prediction," the standardized response to a prediction error, and the mechanism that maintains consistency across successive updates. Bayesian cognitive science attempts to subsume all uncertainty under probabilistic belief updating, but it presupposes a closed hypothesis space and provides no generative account of how the objects over which probabilities are distributed become discrete, identifiable referents in the first place. This paper introduces Predictive Set Theory (PST), a formal generative framework that reconstructs cognitive architecture from first principles. PST anchors cognition in a minimal set of operations---a sensor formalized as an identity function, set-theoretic state refresh, and three fundamental forms of reference chains (reference, counter-reference, and semi-reference)---and rigorously derives core cognitive functions including state sequences, demand, comparison, efficiency, and finite-horizon probabilistic planning. Rather than modeling neural mechanisms, PST constitutes a design specification for any system that must maintain internal consistency while acting under incomplete information and irreversible risk. The framework offers novel resolutions to classical problems such as Russell's paradox, the cognitive status of Gödelian incompleteness, the grounding of negative feedback, and the comprehension of film editing. The primary purpose of this paper is to establish, through the public academic record, the originality and completeness of the Predictive Set Theory framework.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces Predictive Set Theory (PST), a formal generative framework that reconstructs cognitive architecture from first principles using minimal operations: a sensor formalized as an identity function, set-theoretic state refresh, and three types of reference chains (reference, counter-reference, semi-reference). PST derives core cognitive functions like state sequences, demand, comparison, efficiency, and finite-horizon probabilistic planning, and offers novel solutions to classical problems including Russell's paradox and Gödelian incompleteness.
AI.motivation: Predictive processing theories lack operational definitions for prediction structure, standard prediction-error responses, and consistency mechanisms across updates. Bayesian cognitive science presupposes closed hypothesis spaces and fails to explain how probabilistic referents become discrete and identifiable. PST aims to fill these gaps with a generative formal framework.
AI.method: PST is constructed from foundational set operations: a sensor as an identity function, set-theoretic state refresh, and three reference chain forms. From these, it rigorously derives cognitive functions including state sequences, demand, comparison, efficiency, and finite-horizon probabilistic planning. The framework is designed as a specification rather than a neural model.
AI.result: PST provides novel resolutions to classical problems including Russell's paradox, the cognitive status of Gödelian incompleteness, grounding of negative feedback, and comprehension of film editing. The paper's primary purpose is establishing the originality and completeness of PST through the public academic record.
AI.conclusion: PST constitutes a design specification for any system that must maintain internal consistency while acting under incomplete information and irreversible risk, offering a formal generative foundation for cognitive architecture beyond both predictive processing and Bayesian frameworks.

title: Experimental access to molarity's blind spot in macroscopic assays
comment: 58 pages, 6 figures. Companion paper submitted simultaneously: "A concentration-independent paradigm rendering weak interactions inherently quantifiable" (M. Yoshimura et al.). Cross-references to the companion arXiv identifier will be added in v2
summary: Chemical kinetics has long inferred local molecular behaviour through the flask-and-molarity pairing, where well-mixed concentrations serve as the experimental readout. Yet many biological reactions occur in structured environments. Researchers have long recognized that concentration may not carry the same operational meaning in such environments, but even local concepts such as effective molarity usually translate local effects back into a single value with units of concentration. What has been missing is the complementary path: a bench-compatible way to make local structure an experimental variable, rather than only a correction to molarity. Here we show a chemistry-geometry crossover that the flask-and-molarity interface could not make visible. In the micromolar-or-weaker affinity regime, inhibition can switch sharply out of the familiar concentration-and-affinity mode: chemical binding strength no longer determines the response, and the shape of the target's local space does. A bench-compatible interface made this switch measurable by separating bulk dose from local geometry. This blind spot arose from the hidden premise that macroscopic pooling makes a structured local state readable as a single local concentration. The chemistry-geometry crossover breaks that premise: in a structured target environment, a macroscopic assay can remain sensitive to the probability distribution of local states, so collapsing that distribution to one concentration-valued number removes the geometric control axis from the readout. By preserving that axis in the experiment, the interface bypasses molarity's hidden bottleneck and provides a routine experimental route to remeasure and reinterpret molecular interactions in structured space.

AI.tldr: The paper reveals a chemistry-geometry crossover in weak-affinity molecular interactions where local spatial structure, not chemical binding strength, determines inhibition response in the micromolar-or-weaker regime. The authors demonstrate that traditional flask-and-molarity approaches collapse structured local states into a single concentration value, obscuring a geometric control axis that a bench-compatible interface can preserve and measure.
AI.motivation: Traditional chemical kinetics relies on well-mixed flask conditions and molarity as the experimental readout, but many biological reactions occur in structured environments where concentration may not carry the same operational meaning. Current approaches like effective molarity translate local effects back into concentration units, but no bench-compatible method exists to make local structure itself an experimental variable rather than just a correction to molarity.
AI.method: The authors construct a bench-compatible experimental interface that separates bulk dose from local geometry, enabling measurement of the distribution of local states rather than collapsing them to a single concentration-valued number. This allows the geometric axis to be preserved as an independent experimental control.
AI.result: In the micromolar-or-weaker affinity regime, the authors observe a sharp crossover where inhibition no longer follows the familiar concentration-and-affinity mode. Instead, the shape of the target's local space determines the response, bypassing chemical binding strength as the controlling factor. This chemistry-geometry crossover is invisible to traditional flask-and-molarity measurements.
AI.conclusion: Macroscopic assays can remain sensitive to the probability distribution of local states in structured environments, so collapsing that distribution into a single concentration value removes the geometric control axis from the readout. By preserving this axis, the interface provides a routine experimental route to remeasure and reinterpret molecular interactions in structured space, revealing a hidden bottleneck in molarity-based approaches.

title: A concentration-independent paradigm rendering weak interactions inherently quantifiable
comment: 95 pages, 6 figures, 19 supplementary figures. Companion paper submitted simultaneously: "Experimental access to molarity's blind spot in macroscopic assays" (F. Matsuda, M. Yoshimura, S. Ikeda, D. Fujita). Cross-references to the companion arXiv identifier will be added in v2
summary: A vast class of weak, millimolar-affinity molecular interactions governs cellular function, yet their quantitative characterization has remained largely beyond conventional methods. For over a century, biochemistry has worked within a concentration-based framework where molarity scales with molecular number per volume (N/V), and experiments have usually, often implicitly, changed concentration by moving N while holding V fixed. The weak-interaction measurement bottleneck arises from this paradigm: reading weak binding through bulk concentration requires concentrations beyond practical limits, a framework constraint rather than one of instrumental sensitivity. Here we show that shifting experimental control from N to accessible volume V overcomes this bottleneck and opens previously intractable affinity ranges through nanoscale spatial confinement. Controlling V means controlling what biochemists have called "local concentration" and "proximity effects," recasting these long-ambiguous notions as quantitative variables grounded in first principles. Implemented in DNA nanocavities, the approach showed that geometric arrangement alone can override solution-phase binding hierarchies. The same spatial control quantified a protein-peptide interaction of order 10 mM from femtomoles per well, totalling under a picomole per titration. Even so, a standard plate reader gave a signal-to-noise ratio near 10^3, leaving headroom for still weaker interactions. The affinity-and-geometry readout also enabled rational screening for protein-protein-interaction modulators, identifying compounds that enhance weak associations by reweighting local encounters rather than binding tightly on their own or forming a stable ternary complex. Together, this volume-based paradigm and its implementation provide a general strategy for probing and modulating previously inaccessible biochemical phenomena.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces a volume-based paradigm for measuring weak molecular interactions by shifting experimental control from concentration (N/V, varying N) to accessible volume (varying V) via nanoscale spatial confinement. Implemented in DNA nanocavities, this approach enables quantitative characterization of millimolar-affinity interactions, overrides solution-phase binding hierarchies through geometry alone, and enables rational screening for protein-protein interaction modulators.
AI.motivation: Weak, millimolar-affinity molecular interactions govern cellular function but have remained largely unquantifiable. The bottleneck is a paradigm constraint: the concentration-based framework requires impractical concentrations to read weak binding through bulk assays. This is not a sensitivity issue but a fundamental limitation of the N/V framework where experiments vary N while holding V fixed.
AI.method: The authors shift experimental control from molecular number N to accessible volume V, leveraging nanoscale spatial confinement to control "local concentration" and "proximity effects" as quantitative first-principles variables. The approach is implemented in DNA nanocavities, where geometric arrangement controls binding outcomes, allowing quantification of weak interactions (e.g., 10 mM protein-peptide interactions) from femtomoles of material, and enabling affinity-and-geometry readouts for rational screening of protein-protein interaction modulators.
AI.result: The approach demonstrated that geometric arrangement alone can override solution-phase binding hierarchies. It quantified a 10 mM protein-peptide interaction using femtomoles per well (under a picomole per titration) with a standard plate reader achieving signal-to-noise ratio near 10^3. It also enabled identification of compounds that enhance weak protein-protein associations by reweighting local encounters rather than binding tightly or forming stable ternary complexes.
AI.conclusion: The volume-based paradigm provides a general strategy for probing and modulating previously inaccessible biochemical phenomena, overcoming the century-old concentration-based measurement framework's constraints on weak interaction analysis.

title: Modelling temporal dynamics of suicidal ideation and behaviour across pre- to early adolescence using a Markov framework
summary: Understanding the dynamics of suicidal ideation and behaviour in youth and the factors associated with transitions from thoughts to behaviours is critical for early identification, monitoring, and prevention. Using longitudinal self-report data from the Adolescent Brain Cognitive Development (ABCD) Study (n = 11,864) spanning ages 9 to 13 years, we developed a time-inhomogeneous discrete-time Markov chain framework to model transitions across eight states defined by suicidal ideation and behaviour and the co-reported presence or absence of non-suicidal self-injury (NSSI). The framework enables inference of year-to-year and multi-year transition probabilities, quantification of transition stability and uncertainty, and statistical comparison of transition likelihoods. We identified structured but developmentally changing transition patterns, including a generally high probability of recovery to a no-report state following reports of suicidal ideation or behaviour. Co-reported lifetime NSSI marked a distinct trajectory profile characterized by both greater risk and lower predictability: children with NSSI were more likely to transition to or persist in suicidal behaviour, were less likely to recover to a no-report state, and exhibited greater uncertainty in their transition likelihoods compared to those reporting suicidal ideation and/or behaviour alone. These findings suggest that NSSI marks not only elevated risk but also greater trajectory instability during pre- to early adolescence. By estimating probabilities of escalation, remission, persistence, and fluctuation in longitudinal cohort data, the framework provides a systematic, interpretable, and scalable approach to characterising suicidal trajectory dynamics in large, sparse mental health datasets, with potential to inform future research on monitoring, early prevention, and time-varying risk in youth mental health.

AI.tldr: This paper develops a time-inhomogeneous discrete-time Markov chain framework using ABCD Study data (n=11,864, ages 9-13) to model transitions across eight states of suicidal ideation/behaviour and NSSI co-occurrence, revealing that NSSI marks both greater suicide risk and lower trajectory predictability in youth.
AI.motivation: Understanding how suicidal ideation transitions to behaviour in youth and identifying factors associated with these transitions is critical for early identification, monitoring, and prevention of suicide risk in adolescents.
AI.method: A time-inhomogeneous discrete-time Markov chain framework was applied to longitudinal self-report data from the ABCD Study, modelling transitions across eight states defined by suicidal ideation, behaviour, and co-reported NSSI. The framework supports inference of year-to-year and multi-year transition probabilities, quantification of stability and uncertainty, and statistical comparison of transition likelihoods.
AI.result: Structured but developmentally changing transition patterns were found, with generally high probability of recovery following suicidal ideation/behaviour reports. Children with co-reported NSSI showed a distinct profile: higher likelihood of transitioning to or persisting in suicidal behaviour, lower recovery probability, and greater uncertainty in transition likelihoods compared to those without NSSI.
AI.conclusion: NSSI marks not only elevated suicide risk but also greater trajectory instability during pre- to early adolescence. The framework offers a systematic, interpretable, and scalable approach for characterising suicidal trajectory dynamics in large, sparse mental health datasets, with potential to inform monitoring, early prevention, and time-varying risk research.

title: Scaling an Autoregressive Transformer for Single-Cell Generation
summary: We study a self-supervised generation task for single-cell gene expression vectors: given a set of vectors from a cell type, we aim to generate additional gene expression vectors of that cell type. For this task we characterize both the biological fidelity of the generated gene expression vectors and the scaling behavior of the pretraining loss. The model is a causal transformer paired with a learned quantized VAE tokenizer, trained with a cross-entropy loss. To evaluate the model, we condition it on held-out gene expression vectors of a cell type and generate vectors of gene expression, comparing the resulting distribution over gene expression vectors to the ground truth distribution of that cell type. We study the scaling properties of the proposed architecture by varying the number of trained parameters and the amount of training data. To our knowledge, we find the first jointly-fit two-exponent scaling law and compute-optimal frontier for a single-cell foundation model. Finally, we discuss how this pretrained model could be finetuned for perturbation response prediction.

AI.tldr: This paper presents a self-supervised generation task for single-cell gene expression vectors using a causal transformer with a quantized VAE tokenizer, and characterizes both biological fidelity and scaling behavior, including the first jointly-fit two-exponent scaling law for a single-cell foundation model.
AI.motivation: The authors aim to enable generation of additional gene expression vectors for a given cell type, which is valuable for data augmentation and understanding cellular heterogeneity, while also studying how foundation models scale for single-cell data.
AI.method: The model is a causal transformer paired with a learned quantized VAE tokenizer, trained with cross-entropy loss. Evaluation is performed by conditioning on held-out gene expression vectors of a cell type and generating new vectors, comparing generated distributions to ground truth. Scaling is studied by varying model parameters and training data size.
AI.result: The paper finds the first jointly-fit two-exponent scaling law and compute-optimal frontier for a single-cell foundation model, while also characterizing biological fidelity of generated gene expression vectors.
AI.conclusion: The pretrained model shows promise for scaling in single-cell genomics, and the authors discuss potential fine-tuning for perturbation response prediction tasks.

title: A Landau-Ginzburg Phenomenology of Sleep-Stage Transitions
comment: 23 pages, 5 figures, 7 tables. Theoretical and computational framework; no new empirical data
summary: Sleep staging provides a reproducible clinical description, but it does not by itself explain why some boundaries are abrupt while others are graded, or why transition windows contain instability, synchrony, and apparent state coexistence. We develop a local Landau-Ginzburg phenomenology in which each boundary is represented by motion in an effective potential of a spatially extended, noisy, dissipative neural field. A latent cortical-ordering coordinate phi is inferred from prespecified EEG/PSG observables through a measurement model designed to avoid circularity. The canonical boundaries are treated separately. Existing data support a fold-like loss of wake stability at sleep onset; whether that fold lies on a globally bistable cusp with hysteresis remains open. N1-to-N2 and N2-to-N3 are posed as continuous-like ordering crossovers, NREM-to-REM as a candidate first-order-like desynchronizing switch, and a possible within-N3 mixed or tricritical-like regime as a speculative hypothesis. The Ginzburg term adds spatial predictions - growth of correlation length and local-to-global recruitment - that are absent from scalar sleep-onset models. We specify the evidence needed to distinguish bifurcation, coexistence, noise-driven escape, smooth crossover, and scoring-induced discontinuity. Illustrative time-dependent Ginzburg-Landau simulations reproduce the proposed signature classes. A synthetic classification experiment partially distinguished six archetypes (cross-validated accuracy 0.49 +/- 0.005; balanced baseline 0.17), with little change under a noise-regime shift. These analyses establish the internal consistency and testability of the framework, not the proposed taxonomy in human sleep. Transition-centered EEG validation is required before clinical or neuromodulation applications are pursued.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a Landau-Ginzburg phenomenological framework to model sleep stage transitions, treating each boundary as motion in an effective potential of a noisy, dissipative neural field. A latent cortical-ordering coordinate is inferred from EEG/PSG observables, with canonical boundaries classified into distinct dynamical archetypes (fold-like sleep onset, continuous crossovers for N1-N2/N2-N3, first-order-like NREM-REM switch, speculative tricritical N3 regime). The framework adds spatial predictions via the Ginzburg term (correlation length growth, local-to-global recruitment) and is validated through simulations and synthetic classification experiments, establishing internal consistency and testability—though not yet human sleep validity.
AI.motivation: Sleep staging is clinically reproducible but fails to explain mechanistic differences between boundaries (abrupt vs. graded transitions, instability, synchrony, state coexistence). The authors aim to develop a physically grounded framework that captures the dynamical nature of these transitions rather than treating stages as discrete states.
AI.method: Develops a local Landau-Ginzburg phenomenology with a latent cortical-ordering coordinate inferred from EEG/PSG via a measurement model designed to avoid circularity. Each boundary is represented by motion in an effective potential of a spatially extended, noisy, dissipative neural field. Uses time-dependent Ginzburg-Landau simulations to reproduce proposed signature classes and a synthetic classification experiment with six archetypes (cross-validated accuracy 0.49, balanced baseline 0.17).
AI.result: Simulations reproduce the proposed signature classes. Synthetic classification partially distinguishes six archetypes (accuracy 0.49 ± 0.005 vs. 0.17 baseline), with robustness to noise-regime shifts. The framework generates specific spatial predictions (correlation length growth, local-to-global recruitment) absent from scalar models, and specifies evidence needed to distinguish competing dynamical explanations.
AI.conclusion: The framework is internally consistent and testable, but does not yet establish validity for human sleep. Transition-centered EEG validation is required before clinical or neuromodulation applications. Key open question: whether the fold at sleep onset lies on a globally bistable cusp with hysteresis.

title: Spatial proteomics guided by H&E-based AI reveals recurrence-risk niches in triple-negative breast cancer
comment: Triple-negative breast cancer (TNBC), Recurrence, Digital pathology, Artificial intelligence, Spatial proteomics, Tumor microenvironment
summary: Deep learning models can predict cancer recurrence from H&E stained slides, but the localized molecular states underlying these predictions remain largely obscured. Here, we developed an outcome informed spatial pathology framework in TNBC that integrates AI generated recurrence risk heatmaps with mass spectrometry based spatial proteomics. In a cohort of 156 patients, distribution based aggregation of high scoring patches achieved an AUC of 0.77 and a C-index of 0.77 in an independent test cohort. Bulk proteomics associated high image derived risk with cell cycle and genome maintenance programs and low risk with immune activation. High and low risk patches coexisted within the same tumor compartment and displayed distinct nuclear and architectural features, revealing intratumoral heterogeneity beyond tissue compartment identity. We then used the heatmaps as coordinate level guides to physically isolate and profile 46 AI defined tumor regions from two recurrence patients. Spatial proteomic profiling revealed a concordant molecular contrast across both patients: mitotic programs were enriched in high risk regions and immune and antigen presentation programs in low risk regions. A 13 protein composite derived from these spatial contrasts showed a trend toward poorer recurrence-free survival with increasing scores in an expanded cohort, while the corresponding transcript based composite stratified recurrence free survival in the independent METABRIC TNBC cohort. Integrating the protein composite with the H&E derived risk score improved the out of bag C-index from 0.679 to 0.739 and enhanced time dependent discrimination at 3 and 5 years. Together, these findings define a new role for outcome trained AI models as spatially explicit experimental guides that connect prognostic morphology with localized molecular states and advance biologically grounded, multiscale biomarker discovery in TNBC.

AI.tldr: An outcome-informed spatial pathology framework integrates AI-generated recurrence risk heatmaps with mass spectrometry-based spatial proteomics in TNBC, achieving AUC 0.77 and C-index 0.77, and revealing concordant molecular contrasts (mitotic programs in high-risk, immune programs in low-risk regions) with a 13-protein composite improving prognostic discrimination.
AI.motivation: Deep learning models can predict cancer recurrence from H&E slides, but the localized molecular states underlying these predictions remain obscured, limiting biological interpretability and translation of these prognostic models.
AI.method: Integrated AI-generated recurrence risk heatmaps with mass spectrometry-based spatial proteomics. Used distribution-based aggregation of high-scoring patches, bulk proteomics association, and heatmap-guided physical isolation/profiling of 46 AI-defined tumor regions from two recurrence patients.
AI.result: Achieved AUC 0.77 and C-index 0.77 in independent test cohort. High-risk regions enriched in mitotic and cell cycle programs; low-risk enriched in immune/antigen presentation programs. A 13-protein composite trended toward poorer RFS and improved out-of-bag C-index from 0.679 to 0.739 when combined with H&E risk score.
AI.conclusion: Outcome-trained AI models can serve as spatially explicit experimental guides connecting prognostic morphology with localized molecular states, advancing biologically grounded multiscale biomarker discovery in TNBC.

title: Active wetting/de-wetting of focal adhesions on viscoelastic substrates
summary: Cell adhesion to viscoelastic substrates is mediated by focal adhesions (FAs), which dynamically couple actomyosin contractility to the extracellular matrix. Although substrate stress relaxation is known to regulate adhesion stability and cell migration, a predictive physical framework linking viscoelasticity to force transmission and adhesion dynamics remains lacking. Here we review briefly what is known about the active wetting and de-wetting of FAs on viscoelastic substrates and synthesize existing experimental and theoretical work into a two-timescale physical framework to describe the phenomena reported. At short timescales, oscillatory actomyosin-driven displacements are transmitted through molecular clutches, leading to frequency-dependent energy transfer to the substrate. We show that this transfer is maximized at an optimal frequency set by a balance between elastic energy storage and viscous dissipation, establishing a resonance-like mechanism that selects both the effective FA stiffness and traction force amplitude. At longer timescales, this mechanically optimal state couples to adhesion remodelling through an effective surface tension, enabling FA growth and disassembly to be interpreted as active wetting and de-wetting processes. The model predicts that adhesion stability and steady-state size are controlled by substrate stiffness and viscoelastic timescales, as well as mechanosensitive feedback mediated by Piezo1-dependent calcium signalling.

AI.tldr: This paper reviews cell adhesion to viscoelastic substrates and proposes a two-timescale physical framework linking substrate stress relaxation to focal adhesion (FA) dynamics, force transmission, and adhesion stability.
AI.motivation: Although substrate stress relaxation is known to regulate adhesion stability and cell migration, there is a lack of a predictive physical framework connecting viscoelasticity to force transmission and adhesion dynamics.
AI.method: The authors synthesize existing experimental and theoretical work into a two-timescale framework: (1) at short timescales, oscillatory actomyosin-driven displacements transmit through molecular clutches, with frequency-dependent energy transfer maximized at an optimal resonance-like frequency; (2) at longer timescales, this mechanically optimal state couples to adhesion remodeling via effective surface tension, modeled as active wetting/de-wetting.
AI.result: The model shows energy transfer to the substrate is maximized at an optimal frequency balancing elastic energy storage and viscous dissipation, selecting both effective FA stiffness and traction force amplitude. It predicts adhesion stability and steady-state size depend on substrate stiffness, viscoelastic timescales, and Piezo1-dependent calcium signaling feedback.
AI.conclusion: FA growth and disassembly can be interpreted as active wetting and de-wetting processes, providing a unified physical framework where adhesion stability and size are governed by substrate viscoelasticity and mechanosensitive feedback.

title: Omega-S: A Functional Resilience Index for LLM Fine-Tuning
comment: 15 pages of main text plus appendices; 12 tables. Code, per-seed data and all negative results at https://github.com/BiomeMakers/OmegaS-LLM
summary:
Fine-tuning a large language model on new data degrades what it previously learned. We present Omega-S, a drop-in penalty computed from the weight matrix alone: it needs no previous-task data, no Fisher matrix and no stored copy of the old weights. It is three lines in an existing training loop and adds under 4% to the cost of a step.
  Retention. On Llama-3-8B with LoRA, fine-tuned from code to prose and measured by HumanEval over ten seeds, Omega-S retains more of the original capability than no regularisation on 9 of 10 seeds (0.173 -> 0.238 absolute pass@1; sign test one-sided p=0.011, Wilcoxon p=0.006), as a retention ratio, 62.9% -> 84.1%. It also beats tuned weight decay on 10 of 10 seeds (p=0.002) and tuned EWC on 8 of 10 (p=0.014), every arm re-measured in the same session.
  Mechanism, measured rather than asserted. Omega-S is topological by construction, its objective built from Tr(A^3), but we measured which of its four factors actually moves and three do not: their elasticity with respect to the weights is at or below 1e-4, against 9e-3 for the degree-variance term. As implemented, the composite reduces to a penalty on the variance of node degrees, which means row magnitude in square modules and directional alignment in non-square ones. We report this because a method whose name promises one thing and whose gradient does another should say so. We also enumerate the open design choices, including a contrast-preserving construction that does what it was designed to do and makes retention worse on all ten seeds.
  Repeating an identical configuration, same seed and same hardware, gives a standard deviation of 0.104 in retention ratio. We have not found this quantified for low-rank fine-tuning of language models, and it bounds every seed-paired comparison in this literature, ours included.
  Code, per-seed results and the full record of negative results are available.

AI.tldr: Omega-S is a drop-in regularization penalty computed solely from the weight matrix that preserves prior capabilities during LLM fine-tuning, retaining 84.1% of original capability vs 62.9% without regularization on Llama-3-8B, while being cheap (<4% step cost) and transparent about its actual mechanism.
AI.motivation: Fine-tuning large language models on new data causes catastrophic forgetting — degradation of previously learned capabilities. Existing solutions (EWC, Fisher-based methods, stored weights) are expensive or require access to prior-task data. The authors seek a simple, data-free penalty that prevents forgetting.
AI.method: Omega-S is a penalty computed from the weight matrix alone, built from Tr(A^3) (a topological construction). It requires no prior-task data, no Fisher matrix, no stored old weights, and adds only ~3 lines to a training loop with <4% computational overhead. The authors empirically dissect which of its four factors actually contributes to retention, finding it effectively reduces to a penalty on the variance of node degrees.
AI.result: On Llama-3-8B with LoRA fine-tuning from code to prose: retains more capability than no regularization on 9/10 seeds (pass@1 0.173→0.238), improving retention ratio from 62.9% to 84.1%. Beats tuned weight decay on 10/10 seeds and tuned EWC on 8/10 seeds. The mechanism analysis shows only the degree-variance term is active (elasticity 9e-3 vs ≤1e-4 for others). Reproducibility variance is quantified at σ=0.104 retention ratio.
AI.conclusion: Omega-S offers a simple, cheap, and effective regularization for preventing catastrophic forgetting during fine-tuning, with honest reporting of its true mechanism and the variance that limits all comparisons in this literature. Code and full negative results are shared.
